The Recap

Q2: The Pollination

Every interaction lands in Magic, Mediocrity, or Misery. A quick refresh on the work we did in May, because today assumes you have been living it for ninety days.

01 The Three States

Magic.
Mediocrity.
Misery.

Every visit, call, and invoice lands in exactly one. Misery is loud. Mediocrity is the silent killer. Magic is the neighbor hearing about us.

02 The Moves

Anticipate. Communicate. Close the Loop.

Three patterns of effortless service, plus the Empowered Yes: the person closest to the customer makes it right. We asked for Austin's dollar amount. Today we ask what you found.

03 Personal Commitment

Your 90-Day Card.

"I will pollinate the Austin field by ____." You wrote it. You read it to a partner. We promised to open today by reading them aloud. We keep our promises.

The Pivot

The Lens Turns to What Lingers.

In February we worked on what happens between us. In May we worked on what happens at the doorstep. Today we work on what happens after the truck pulls away. The customer stands in their kitchen. The invoice is paid. The tech is three streets over. And something is still there. A feeling. A great story forming. A name they will either repeat to a neighbor or never say again. The aftertaste is the only part of the visit the customer keeps.

Shep Hyken · Still With Us · The Verdict, Upgraded

The Moment of Magic, one step further

Hyken gave us the doorstep. A Moment of Magic earns the next visit. A Moment of Magic that lingers earns the next customer. Same moment. Same tech. Same doorstep. The only difference is what we do in the seventy-two hours after we leave.

The Aftertaste

The Moment of Magic, One Week Later.

Hyken's three states from May, measured after we leave. The customer does not remember the visit. They remember what the visit left behind.

Misery leaves it

Bitter

They are still talking about it. To the neighbor. On the review site. In the group text. The story has our name in it and we are the villain.

"I would warn you."
Mediocrity leaves it

Bland

They cannot remember who came out. They will shop the next job. We were fine, and fine is forgotten by Thursday.

"Some company. They were fine."
Magic leaves it

Sweet

They repeat the tech's name. They bring us up unprompted. They defend us when a neighbor complains about their guy. We became part of their story.

"You have to call ABC."
ABC Austin · Brand Promise
Care Like Our Own. Highly Trained Team.
Friendly Every Time. Here Tomorrow.
Each and every time. Back up what we do and say today.
The Ladder

Satisfied Is Not the Finish Line.

A satisfied customer got what they paid for. That is the price of admission, not the prize. Advocacy is three rungs up, and every rung is a Moment of Magic we choose to create after the work is done.

Rung One

Satisfied

The work was done right, on time. They feel nothing in particular.

Silent.
→
Rung Two

Loyal

They call us again without shopping. They trust the name.

"I wouldn't call anyone else. See you guys next time."
→
Rung Three

Advocate

They tell the neighbor. They leave the review. They defend us.

"I'll send my neighbor."
→
Rung Four

Legacy

Their kids call us. The whole street calls us. Our name is part of the neighborhood.

"We have always used ABC."
The Mapping

Four Pillars. Four Things That Linger.

In May we mapped each pillar to a Moment of Magic. Today we map each pillar to what the customer says about us a month later, when we are not in the room.

01 Care Like Our Own

"They treat my house like theirs."

The lingering feeling of stewardship. They hand us the gate code. They stop watching over the tech's shoulder. Trust is the aftertaste of care.

02 Highly Trained Team

"I don't get second opinions anymore."

The lingering feeling of confidence. They stop shopping the bid. They repeat what our specialist explained as if it were their own idea.

03 Friendly Every Time

"Can you send the same tech?"

The lingering feeling of being known. They remember a name, and they ask for it. A person, not a ticket, in both directions.

04 Here Tomorrow

"I just call ABC for everything."

The lingering feeling of safety. One number for the whole home. The legacy pillar. It is only earned by what we do after something breaks.

01 Principle One

Dignity at the Doorstep.

Every individual is treated with dignity. Not the ones who earned it. Every one.

After Horst Schulze

The customer in the mobile home and the customer in the Tarrytown mansion. The customer who is rude on the phone. The CSR on her fortieth call. The new tech on his first ride-along. Dignity is not a reward for good behavior. It is the standard we carry in the truck. And it starts inside the hive. Ladies and Gentlemen cannot serve Ladies and Gentlemen if we do not treat our own people that way first.

02 Principle Two

The Empowered Yes.

The person closest to the customer has the authority to make it right, right now, without a phone call. We introduced it in May. We asked one question and sent you home with it: what is Austin's number? Let's review and discuss.

$2,000

Per employee. Per guest. No permission.

The Ritz-Carlton number. Not because problems cost that much. Because the customer standing on the driveway does not have time for us to find a manager.

Ninety Days Later

The Empowered Yes, Revisited.

In May we asked one question: what dollar amount of authority does your Austin team have to make a customer right on the spot? The Ritz-Carlton answer is $2,000 and no phone call. Here is the same Tuesday afternoon, told twice.

Tuesday, 4:55 PM · A Permission Culture

"Let me check with my manager."

The tech nicked a sprinkler line. He knows how to fix it. He also knows he is not allowed to comp a forty-dollar repair without a call. So he calls. The manager is in a meeting. The customer waits on the driveway, arms folded, and hears the word "policy" twice before anyone says "sorry."

Aftertaste: "They had to ask permission to do the right thing."
Tuesday, 4:55 PM · A Yes Culture

"Already handled. My mistake."

Same nick. Same tech. He knows his number. He fixes the line, tells the customer what he did and why, and knocks the repair off the invoice before she asks. He mentions it at the Tuesday meeting and gets a round of applause, not a write-up.

Aftertaste: "That guy owned it. Ask for him next time."

03 Principle Three · From Shep Hyken

The Recovery Paradox.

A customer who has a problem, and watches us fix it well, ends up more loyal than a customer who never had a problem at all. Researchers have measured it for thirty years. Hyken built a career on it. Most home services companies have never heard of it.

"They were fine."
No problem,
no recovery
"Never again."
Problem,
poor recovery
"You have to call ABC."
Problem,
great recovery
The Recovery Paradox · The Austin Translation

They do not judge us by what happened. They judge us by what we did about it.

Shep Hyken · I'll Be Back

The failure is not the end of the story. The failure is where the story gets interesting. Our best advocates are almost always people we once let down. Which means every miss in Austin this week is a Moment of Magic waiting for someone to claim it.

Recovery

Four Moves. In Order. Every Time.

In May we contrasted the common mistake with the Hyken move. Today we make it a sequence your whole team can run without you in the room.

01 Within the Hour

Acknowledge

Surface it before the customer does. Say what happened in plain words, in their words. The clock starts the moment we know, not the moment they call.

02 Human Voice

Apologize

Pick up the phone. Use their name. Own the impact, not the excuse. They do not care about the backorder. They care they took the morning off.

03 The Empowered Yes

Act

Make the remedy bigger than the problem, and make it now. This is where the dollar amount either exists or it does not.

04 Three Days Later

Aftercare

The call nobody expects. "Just checking that it held." The aftertaste is written here, not at the fix. This is the move most companies skip.

From Hyken

Three Moments of Magic Nobody Sees.

In May the Magic happened at the doorstep with the customer watching. The Q3 Magic happens after we leave, when nobody is watching. That is exactly why it lingers.

Magic Moment · Day Three

The Callback

"Just making sure it held." Sixty seconds. No upsell. The customer has never once received this call from a home services company. Now they have.

Anticipate, after the fact.
Magic Moment · The Miss

The Recovery

We broke it, we said so first, we fixed it bigger than we broke it, and we called three days later. The customer tells that story for a decade.

Communicate, when it hurts.
Magic Moment · The Referral

The Thank-You

A neighbor calls because of them. We call them back to say so, by name, from the tech who did the work. Advocates who feel honored advocate again.

Close the loop, twice.

Advocacy

Advocates Are Made, Not Found.

Satisfied customers rarely become advocates on their own. Somebody has to earn the story, ask for the story, and then honor the person who told it.

01 The Move

Earn It

Magic first. Never ask for a review after Mediocrity; you will get an honest one. The ask only works when the customer already has a story to tell.

02 The Move

Ask for It

Right after the "wow," in person, by the person who created it. Not a link on the invoice three days later. "If you know a neighbor who needs this, I would be honored to take care of them too."

03 The Move

Honor It

Thank the referrer by name. Tell the tech whose name showed up in the review. Read the review at the Tuesday meeting. Advocates who feel honored advocate again.

The Manager's Multiplier

You decide what lingers.

Nobody on your team will treat a customer with more dignity than you treat them. Nobody will recover more gracefully than they have watched you recover. Nobody will ask for the story if the story never gets told. The aftertaste your customers keep is the aftertaste your team gets from you.

Three rhythms that fit alongside what you built in May. Examples, not a mandate. Pick what fits your team.

01 Mondays

The Story Hunt

Find one customer from last week who repeated our name to someone. Find out exactly what they said. Write it down.

02 Tuesdays

The Recovery Replay

Take one failure from last week and walk it through Acknowledge, Apologize, Act, Aftercare in front of the team. No blame. Just the replay.

03 Fridays

The Dignity Check

Ask one frontline team member: did anyone get treated with less than dignity this week? A customer, or one of us. Then fix what you hear.

Make It a Rhythm

Principles die in the parking lot.

Unless they have a place on the calendar

Everything you have heard today will be gone by the second Tuesday unless it lives inside a meeting you already run. Not a new meeting. The language goes into the rhythm you already have. Here is what that looks like in Austin.

The Call to Action
Leave It Sweeter.

A worker bee lives about six weeks. The honey it leaves behind never spoils. Every visit your team runs is short. What it leaves in that home can last for years, in either direction. Leave every home, every call, and every teammate a little sweeter than you found them. That is the legacy. That is the honey.
